blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 9.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class XI and in Chapter 5 of the present book, we
discussed how to differentiate a given function $f$ with respect
to an independent variable, i.e., how to find $f'(x)$ for a given
function $f$ at each $x$ in its domain of definition. Further, in
the chapter on Integral Calculus, we discussed how to find
a function $f$ whose derivative is the function $g$, which may
also be formulated as follows:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: For a given function $g$, find a function $f$ such that

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text:
Henri Poincare
(1854-1912 )

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = g(x), \text{ where } y = f(x) \quad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
An equation of the form (1) is known as a differential
equation. A formal definition will be given later.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
These equations arise in a variety of applications, may it be in Physics, Chemistry,
Biology, Anthropology, Geology, Economics etc. Hence, an indepth study of differential
equations has assumed prime importance in all modern scientific investigations.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, we will study some basic concepts related to differential equation,
general and particular solutions of a differential equation, formation of differential
equations, some methods to solve a first order - first degree differential equation and
some applications of differential equations in different areas.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 9.2 Basic Concepts

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We are already familiar with the equations of the type:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$x^2 - 3x + 3 = 0 \quad \dots (1)$$
$$\sin x + \cos x = 0 \quad \dots (2)$$
$$x + y = 7 \quad \dots (3)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider the equation:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$x \frac{dy}{dx} + y = 0 \quad \dots (4)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We see that equations (1), (2) and (3) involve independent and/or dependent variable
(variables) only but equation (4) involves variables as well as derivative of the dependent
variable $y$ with respect to the independent variable $x$. Such an equation is called a
differential equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In general, an equation involving derivative (derivatives) of the dependent variable
with respect to independent variable (variables) is called a differential equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A differential equation involving derivatives of the dependent variable with respect
to only one independent variable is called an ordinary differential equation, e.g.,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$2 \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} + \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^3 = 0 \text{ is an ordinary differential equation} \quad .... (5)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Of course, there are differential equations involving derivatives with respect to
more than one independent variables, called partial differential equations but at this
stage we shall confine ourselves to the study of ordinary differential equations only.
Now onward, we will use the term ‘differential equation’ for ‘ordinary differential
equation’.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Note
1. We shall prefer to use the following notations for derivatives:

$$ \frac{dy}{dx} = y', \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = y'', \frac{d^3y}{dx^3} = y''' $$

2. For derivatives of higher order, it will be inconvenient to use so many dashes

as supersuffix therefore, we use the notation $y_n$ for $n$th order derivative $\frac{d^ny}{dx^n}$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 9.2.1. Order of a differential equation

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Order of a differential equation is defined as the order of the highest order derivative of
the dependent variable with respect to the independent variable involved in the given
differential equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Consider the following differential equations:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = e^x \hspace{150pt} ... (6) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} + y = 0 \qquad \dots (7) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \left( \frac{d^3 y}{dx^3} \right) + x^2 \left( \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} \right)^3 = 0 \qquad \dots (8) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The equations (6), (7) and (8) involve the highest derivative of first, second and
third order respectively. Therefore, the order of these equations are 1, 2 and 3 respectively.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 9.2.2 Degree of a differential equation

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To study the degree of a differential equation, the key point is that the differential
equation must be a polynomial equation in derivatives, i.e., $y'$, $y''$, $y'''$ etc. Consider the
following differential equations:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{d^3 y}{dx^3} + 2 \left( \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} \right)^2 - \frac{dy}{dx} + y = 0 \tag{9} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right) - \sin^2 y = 0 \hfill ... (10) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} + \sin \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right) = 0 \qquad \dots (11) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We observe that equation (9) is a polynomial equation in $y'''$, $y''$ and $y'$, equation (10)
is a polynomial equation in $y'$ (not a polynomial in $y$ though). Degree of such differential
equations can be defined. But equation (11) is not a polynomial equation in $y'$ and
degree of such a differential equation can not be defined.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
By the degree of a differential equation, when it is a polynomial equation in
derivatives, we mean the highest power (positive integral index) of the highest order
derivative involved in the given differential equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In view of the above definition, one may observe that differential equations (6), (7),
(8) and (9) each are of degree one, equation (10) is of degree two while the degree of
differential equation (11) is not defined.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Note Order and degree (if defined) of a differential equation are always
positive integers.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Example 1** Find the order and degree, if defined, of each of the following differential
equations:

(i) $\frac{dy}{dx} - \cos x = 0$

(ii) $xy \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} + x \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^2 - y \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$

(iii) $y''' + y^2 + e^{y'} = 0$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Solution

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) The highest order derivative present in the differential equation is $\frac{dy}{dx}$, so its
order is one. It is a polynomial equation in $y'$ and the highest power raised to $\frac{dy}{dx}$
is one, so its degree is one.

(ii) The highest order derivative present in the given differential equation is $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$, so
its order is two. It is a polynomial equation in $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ and $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and the highest
power raised to $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ is one, so its degree is one.

(iii) The highest order derivative present in the differential equation is $y'''$, so its
order is three. The given differential equation is not a polynomial equation in its
derivatives and so its degree is not defined.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 9.3. General and Particular Solutions of a Differential Equation

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In earlier Classes, we have solved the equations of the type:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$x^2 + 1 = 0 \quad \dots (1)$$
$$\sin^2 x - \cos x = 0 \quad \dots (2)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution of equations (1) and (2) are numbers, real or complex, that will satisfy the
given equation i.e., when that number is substituted for the unknown $x$ in the given
equation, L.H.S. becomes equal to the R.H.S..

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now consider the differential equation $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + y = 0$ ... (3)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In contrast to the first two equations, the solution of this differential equation is a
function $\phi$ that will satisfy it i.e., when the function $\phi$ is substituted for the unknown $y$
(dependent variable) in the given differential equation, L.H.S. becomes equal to R.H.S..

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The curve $y = \phi (x)$ is called the solution curve (integral curve) of the given
differential equation. Consider the function given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$y = \phi (x) = a \sin (x + b), \qquad \dots (4)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
where $a, b \in \mathbf{R}$. When this function and its derivative are substituted in equation (3),
L.H.S. = R.H.S.. So it is a solution of the differential equation (3).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let $a$ and $b$ be given some particular values say $a = 2$ and $b = \frac{\pi}{4}$, then we get a

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: function $y = \phi_1(x) = 2\sin\left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ ... (5)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When this function and its derivative are substituted in equation (3) again
L.H.S. = R.H.S.. Therefore $\phi_1$ is also a solution of equation (3).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Function $\phi$ consists of two arbitrary constants (parameters) $a$, $b$ and it is called
general solution of the given differential equation. Whereas function $\phi_1$ contains no
arbitrary constants but only the particular values of the parameters $a$ and $b$ and hence
is called a particular solution of the given differential equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The solution which contains arbitrary constants is called the general solution
(primitive) of the differential equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The solution free from arbitrary constants i.e., the solution obtained from the general
solution by giving particular values to the arbitrary constants is called a $particular$
$solution$ of the differential equation.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 9.4.1 Differential equations with variables separable

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: A first order-first degree differential equation is of the form

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \mathrm{F}(x, y) \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $F(x, y)$ can be expressed as a product $g(x) h(y)$, where, $g(x)$ is a function of $x$
and $h(y)$ is a function of $y$, then the differential equation (1) is said to be of variable
separable type. The differential equation (1) then has the form

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = h (y) \cdot g (x) \qquad \dots (2) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: If $h(y) \neq 0$, separating the variables, (2) can be rewritten as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{1}{h(y)} dy = g(x) dx \qquad \dots (3) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Integrating both sides of (3), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int \frac{1}{h(y)} dy = \int g(x) dx \tag{4} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus, (4) provides the solutions of given differential equation in the form

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, H ($y$) and G ($x$) are the anti derivatives of $\frac{1}{h(y)}$ and $g(x)$ respectively and
C is the arbitrary constant.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 4 Find the general solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x+1}{2-y}, (y \neq 2)$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x+1}{2-y} \hspace{120pt} ... (1) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Separating the variables in equation (1), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$(2 - y) dy = (x + 1) dx \qquad \dots (2)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Integrating both sides of equation (2), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int (2-y) dy = \int (x+1) dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $x^2 + y^2 + 2x - 4y + C = 0$, where $C = 2C_1$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the general solution of equation (1).

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 5 Find the general solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1+y^2}{1+x^2}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution Since $1 + y^2 \neq 0$, therefore separating the variables, the given differential
equation can be written as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{1+y^2} = \frac{dx}{1+x^2} \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Integrating both sides of equation (1), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int \frac{dy}{1+y^2} = \int \frac{dx}{1+x^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\tan^{-1} y = \tan^{-1} x + C$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the general solution of equation (1).

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 Find the particular solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = -4xy^2$ given
that $y = 1$, when $x = 0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution If $y \neq 0$, the given differential equation can be written as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{y^2} = -4x \ dx \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Integrating both sides of equation (1), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int \frac{dy}{y^2} = -4 \int x \, dx $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting $y = 1$ and $x = 0$ in equation (2), we get, $C = -1$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now substituting the value of C in equation (2), we get the particular solution of the

given differential equation as $y = \frac{1}{2x^2 + 1}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 7 Find the equation of the curve passing through the point $(1, 1)$ whose
differential equation is $x dy = (2x^2 + 1) dx$ $(x \neq 0)$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution The given differential equation can be expressed as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$dy^* = \left( \frac{2x^2 + 1}{x} \right) dx^*$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$dy = \left(2x + \frac{1}{x}\right)dx \quad \dots (1)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Integrating both sides of equation (1), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int dy = \int \left( 2x + \frac{1}{x} \right) dx $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Equation (2) represents the family of solution curves of the given differential equation
but we are interested in finding the equation of a particular member of the family which
passes through the point $(1, 1)$. Therefore substituting $x = 1$, $y = 1$ in equation (2), we
get $C = 0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now substituting the value of C in equation (2) we get the equation of the required
curve as $y = x^2 + \log |x|$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 9.4.2 Homogeneous differential equations

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Consider the following functions in $x$ and $y$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$F_3 (x, y) = \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right), \quad F_4 (x, y) = \sin x + \cos y$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If we replace $x$ and $y$ by $\lambda x$ and $\lambda y$ respectively in the above functions, for any nonzero
constant $\lambda$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$F_1 (\lambda x, \lambda y) = \lambda^2 (y^2 + 2xy) = \lambda^2 F_1 (x, y)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$F_2 (\lambda x, \lambda y) = \lambda (2x - 3y) = \lambda F_2 (x, y)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$F_3 (\lambda x, \lambda y) = \cos \left( \frac{\lambda y}{\lambda x} \right) = \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) = \lambda^0 \ F_3 (x, y)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$F_4 (\lambda x, \lambda y) = \sin \lambda x + \cos \lambda y \neq \lambda^n F_4 (x, y), \text{ for any } n \in \mathbf{N}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, we observe that the functions $\mathrm{F}_1$, $\mathrm{F}_2$, $\mathrm{F}_3$ can be written in the form
$\mathrm{F}(\lambda x, \lambda y) = \lambda^n \mathrm{F}(x, y)$ but $\mathrm{F}_4$ can not be written in this form. This leads to the following
definition:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A function $F(x, y)$ is said to be $homogeneous$ $function$ $of$ $degree$ $n$ if
$F(\lambda x, \lambda y) = \lambda^n F(x, y)$ for any nonzero constant $\lambda$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We note that in the above examples, $\mathrm{F}_1$, $\mathrm{F}_2$, $\mathrm{F}_3$ are homogeneous functions of
degree 2, 1, 0 respectively but $\mathrm{F}_4$ is not a homogeneous function.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We also observe that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$F_1(x, y) = x^2 \left( \frac{y^2}{x^2} + \frac{2y}{x} \right) = x^2 h_1 \left( \frac{y}{x} \right)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $F_1(x, y) = y^2 \left( 1 + \frac{2x}{y} \right) = y^2 h_2 \left( \frac{x}{y} \right)$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$F_2(x, y) = x^1 \left( 2 - \frac{3y}{x} \right) = x^1 h_3 \left( \frac{y}{x} \right)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $F_2(x, y) = y^1 \left( 2 \frac{x}{y} - 3 \right) = y^1 h_4 \left( \frac{x}{y} \right)$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$F_3(x, y) = x^0 \cos\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = x^0 h_5\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathrm{F}_4(x, y) \neq x^n h_6 \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) , \text{ for any } n \in \mathbb{N} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \mathrm{F}_4(x, y) \neq y^n h_7\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)$, for any $n \in \mathbf{N}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, a function F $(x, y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $n$ if

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$F(x, y) = x^n g\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \quad \text{or} \quad y^n h\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A differential equation of the form $\frac{dy}{dx} = \text{F} (x, y)$ is said to be $homogenous$ if
$\text{F}(x, y)$ is a homogenous function of degree zero.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: To solve a homogeneous differential equation of the type

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \mathrm{F}(x, y) = g \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: We make the substitution $y = v.x$ ... (2)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Differentiating equation (2) with respect to $x$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = v + x \frac{dv}{dx} \qquad \dots (3) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting the value of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ from equation (3) in equation (1), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$v + x \frac{dv}{dx} = g(v)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $x \frac{dv}{dx} = g(v) - v$ ... (4)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Separating the variables in equation (4), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dv}{g(v)-v} = \frac{dx}{x} \qquad \dots (5) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Integrating both sides of equation (5), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int \frac{dv}{g(v)-v} = \int \frac{1}{x} dx + C \quad \dots (6) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Equation (6) gives general solution (primitive) of the differential equation (1) when

we replace $v$ by $\frac{y}{x}$.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Note If the homogeneous differential equation is in the form $\frac{dx}{dy} = \mathrm{F}(x, y)$

where, $\mathrm{F}(x, y)$ is homogenous function of degree zero, then we make substitution

$\frac{x}{y} = v$ i.e., $x = vy$ and we proceed further to find the general solution as discussed

above by writing $\frac{dx}{dy} = \mathrm{F}(x, y) = h\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 10 Show that the differential equation $(x-y) \frac{dy}{dx} = x + 2y$ is homogeneous
and solve it.
Solution The given differential equation can be expressed as
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x+2y}{x-y} \quad \dots (1)$$
Let
$$\text{F}(x, y) = \frac{x+2y}{x-y}$$
Now
$$\text{F}(\lambda x, \lambda y) = \frac{\lambda(x+2y)}{\lambda(x-y)} = \lambda^0 \cdot f(x, y)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, $F(x, y)$ is a homogenous function of degree zero. So, the given differential
equation is a homogenous differential equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Alternatively,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \left( \frac{1 + \frac{2y}{x}}{1 - \frac{y}{x}} \right) = g \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \quad \dots (2) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: R.H.S. of differential equation (2) is of the form $g\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)$ and so it is a homogeneous

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
function of degree zero. Therefore, equation (1) is a homogeneous differential equation.
To solve it we make the substitution

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$y = vx \hspace{12em} \dots (3)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Differentiating equation (3) with respect to, $x$ we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = v + x \frac{dv}{dx} \qquad \dots (4) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting the value of $y$ and $\frac{dy}{dx}$ in equation (1) we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$v + x \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1 + 2v}{1 - v}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $x \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1+2v}{1-v} - v$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $x \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v^2 + v + 1}{1 - v}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\frac{v-1}{v^2+v+1}dv = \frac{-dx}{x}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Integrating both sides of equation (5), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int \frac{v-1}{v^2+v+1} dv = -\int \frac{dx}{x} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{or} \quad \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{2v+1}{v^2+v+1} dv - \frac{3}{2} \int \frac{1}{v^2+v+1} dv = -\log |x| + C_1 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\frac{1}{2} \log |v^2 + v + 1| - \frac{3}{2} \int \frac{1}{\left(v + \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2} dv = -\log |x| + C_1$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\frac{1}{2} \log |v^2 + v + 1| - \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2v + 1}{\sqrt{3}} \right) = -\log |x| + C_1$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\frac{1}{2} \log |v^2 + v + 1| + \frac{1}{2} \log x^2 = \sqrt{3} \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2v + 1}{\sqrt{3}} \right) + C_1$ (Why?)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Replacing $v$ by $\frac{y}{x}$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\frac{1}{2} \log \left| \frac{y^2}{x^2} + \frac{y}{x} + 1 \right| + \frac{1}{2} \log x^2 = \sqrt{3} \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2y + x}{\sqrt{3}x} \right) + C_1$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\frac{1}{2} \log \left| \left( \frac{y^2}{x^2} + \frac{y}{x} + 1 \right) x^2 \right| = \sqrt{3} \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2y + x}{\sqrt{3}x} \right) + C_1$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\log \left|\left(y^{2}+x y+x^{2}\right)\right|=2 \sqrt{3} \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{2 y+x}{\sqrt{3} x}\right)+2 \mathrm{C}_{1}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\log \left|\left(x^{2}+x y+y^{2}\right)\right|=2 \sqrt{3} \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2 y}{\sqrt{3} x}\right)+C$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the general solution of the differential equation (1)

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 11 Show that the differential equation $x \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \frac{dy}{dx} = y \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) + x$ is
homogeneous and solve it.
Solution The given differential equation can be written as

$$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) + x}{x \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right)} \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: It is a differential equation of the form $\frac{dy}{dx} = \mathrm{F}(x, y)$ .

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Here $F(x, y) = \frac{y \cos \left(\frac{y}{x}\right) + x}{x \cos \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Replacing $x$ by $\lambda x$ and $y$ by $\lambda y$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$F(\lambda x, \lambda y) = \frac{\lambda \left[ y \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) + x \right]}{\lambda \left( x \cos \frac{y}{x} \right)} = \lambda^0 [F(x, y)]$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus, $F(x, y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, the given differential equation is a homogeneous differential equation.
To solve it we make the substitution

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$y = vx \qquad \dots (2)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Differentiating equation (2) with respect to $x$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = v + x \frac{dv}{dx} \qquad \dots (3) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting the value of $y$ and $\frac{dy}{dx}$ in equation (1), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$v + x \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v \cos v + 1}{\cos v}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $x \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v \cos v + 1}{\cos v} - v$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $x \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1}{\cos v}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\cos v dv = \frac{dx}{x}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $\int \cos v \, dv = \int \frac{1}{x} \, dx$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
or $\sin v = \log |x| + \log |C|$
or $\sin v = \log |Cx|$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Replacing $v$ by $\frac{y}{x}$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \sin \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) = \log |Cx| $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the general solution of the differential equation (1).

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 12 Show that the differential equation $2y e^{\frac{x}{y}} dx + \left( y - 2x e^{\frac{x}{y}} \right) dy = 0$ is
homogeneous and find its particular solution, given that, $x = 0$ when $y = 1$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution The given differential equation can be written as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{2x e^{\bar{y}} - y}{2y e^{\frac{x}{y}}} \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Let $F(x, y) = \frac{2xe^{\frac{x}{y}} - y}{2ye^{\frac{x}{y}}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Then
$$F(\lambda x, \lambda y) = \frac{\lambda \left( 2xe^{\frac{x}{y}} - y \right)}{\lambda \left( 2ye^{\frac{x}{y}} \right)} = \lambda^0 [F(x, y)]$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, $F(x, y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero. Therefore, the given
differential equation is a homogeneous differential equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: To solve it, we make the substitution

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:

Differentiating equation (2) with respect to $y$, we get

blocks.text:
Example 13 Show that the family of curves for which the slope of the tangent at any


point $(x, y)$ on it is $\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2xy}$, is given by $x^2 - y^2 = cx$.


Solution We know that the slope of the tangent at any point on a curve is $\frac{dy}{dx}$.


Therefore, $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^2 + y^2}{2xy}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1 + \frac{y^2}{x^2}}{\frac{2y}{x}} \dots (1)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Clearly, (1) is a homogenous differential equation. To solve it we make substitution

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Differentiating $y = vx$ with respect to $x$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = v + x \frac{dv}{dx} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $v+x \frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{1+v^{2}}{2v}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $x \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1-v^2}{2v}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{2v}{1-v^2} dv = \frac{dx}{x} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\frac{2v}{v^2-1}dv = -\frac{dx}{x}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $$\int \frac{2v}{v^2-1} dv = -\int \frac{1}{x} dx$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\log |v^2 - 1| = -\log |x| + \log |C_1|$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\log \left|\left(v^{2}-1\right)(x)\right|=\log \left|C_{1}\right|$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Replacing $v$ by $\frac{y}{x}$ , we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \left( \frac{y^2}{x^2} - 1 \right) x = \pm C_1 $$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 9.4.3 Linear differential equations

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: A differential equation of the from

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
where, P and Q are constants or functions of $x$ only, is known as a first order linear
differential equation. Some examples of the first order linear differential equation are

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \frac{dy}{dx} + y = \sin x $$

$$ \frac{dy}{dx} + \left( \frac{1}{x} \right) y = e^x $$

$$ \frac{dy}{dx} + \left( \frac{y}{x \log x} \right) = \frac{1}{x} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Another form of first order linear differential equation is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dx}{dy} + \mathbf{P}_1 x = \mathbf{Q}_1 $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
where, $P_1$ and $Q_1$ are constants or functions of $y$ only. Some examples of this type of
differential equation are

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dx}{dy} + x = \cos y $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dx}{dy} + \frac{-2x}{y} = y^2 e^{-y} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: To solve the first order linear differential equation of the type

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q \tag{1} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Multiply both sides of the equation by a function of $x$ say $g(x)$ to get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$g(x) \frac{dy}{dx} + \mathrm{P} \cdot (g(x)) y = \mathrm{Q} \cdot g(x) \qquad \dots (2)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Choose $g(x)$ in such a way that R.H.S. becomes a derivative of $y \cdot g(x)$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e. $g(x) \frac{dy}{dx} + \text{P} \cdot g(x) y = \frac{d}{dx} [y \cdot g(x)]$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $g(x) \frac{dy}{dx} + \text{P} \cdot g(x) y = g(x) \frac{dy}{dx} + y g'(x)$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\Rightarrow$                                     P.g $(x) = g' (x)$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$P = \frac{g'(x)}{g(x)}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \int P dx = \int \frac{g'(x)}{g(x)} dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\int \mathrm{P} \cdot d x=\log (g(x))$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $g(x) = e^{\int P \, dx}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
On multiplying the equation (1) by $g(x) = e^{\int P \, dx}$, the L.H.S. becomes the derivative
of some function of $x$ and $y$. This function $g(x) = e^{\int P \, dx}$ is called Integrating Factor
(I.F.) of the given differential equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting the value of $g(x)$ in equation (2), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ e^{\int \mathrm{P} \, dx} \frac{dy}{dx} + \mathrm{P} e^{\int \mathrm{P} \, dx} y = \mathrm{Q} \cdot e^{\int \mathrm{P} \, dx} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(ye^{\int P_{dx}}\right) = Qe^{\int P_{dx}}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ y \cdot e^{\int \mathrm{P} \, dx} = \int \left( \mathrm{Q} \cdot e^{\int \mathrm{P} \, dx} \right) dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $y = e^{-\int_{\mathrm{P} \, dx} \cdot \int} \left( \mathrm{Q} \cdot e^{\int_{\mathrm{P} \, dx} \right) dx + \mathrm{C}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the general solution of the differential equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Steps involved to solve first order linear differential equation:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) Write the given differential equation in the form $\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$ where P, Q are
constants or functions of $x$ only.
(ii) Find the Integrating Factor (I.F) $= e^{\int P dx}$ .
(iii) Write the solution of the given differential equation as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$y (\text{I.F}) = \int (\text{Q} \times \text{I.F}) dx + \text{C}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In case, the first order linear differential equation is in the form $\frac{dx}{dy} + \mathrm{P_1}x = \mathrm{Q_1}$,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:

Example 14 Find the general solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} - y = \cos x$ .

Solution Given differential equation is of the form

$$\frac{dy}{dx} + \text{P}y = \text{Q} , \text{ where } \text{P} = -1 \text{ and } \text{Q} = \cos x$$

Therefore $\text{I. F} = e^{\int -1 dx} = e^{-x}$

Multiplying both sides of equation by I.F, we get

$$e^{-x} \frac{dy}{dx} - e^{-x} y = e^{-x} \cos x$$

or $$\frac{dy}{dx} \left( y e^{-x} \right) = e^{-x} \cos x$$

On integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we get

$$y e^{-x} = \int e^{-x} \cos x \, dx + \text{C} \quad \dots (1)$$

Let $\text{I} = \int e^{-x} \cos x \, dx$

$$= \cos x \left( \frac{e^{-x}}{-1} \right) - \int (-\sin x) (-e^{-x}) \, dx$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = -\cos x e^{-x} - \int \sin x e^{-x} dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = -\cos x e^{-x} - \left[ \sin x(-e^{-x}) - \int \cos x (-e^{-x}) dx \right] $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = -\cos x e^{-x} + \sin x e^{-x} - \int \cos x e^{-x} dx $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
or
or
$$ \mathrm{I} = - e^{-x} \cos x + \sin x e^{-x} - \mathrm{I} $$
$$ 2\mathrm{I} = (\sin x - \cos x) e^{-x} $$

blocks.text: or $I = \frac{(\sin x - \cos x)e^{-x}}{2}$

Example 15 Find the general solution of the differential equation $x \frac{dy}{dx} + 2y = x^2$ $(x \neq 0)$ .

Solution The given differential equation is

$$x \frac{dy}{dx} + 2y = x^2 \quad \dots \quad (1)$$

Dividing both sides of equation (1) by $x$, we get

$$\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{2}{x} y = x$$

which is a linear differential equation of the type $\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$ , where $P = \frac{2}{x}$ and $Q = x$.

So $I.F = e^{\int_{e}^{2} \frac{dx}{x} = e^{2 \log x} = e^{\log x^2} = x^2}$ [as $e^{\log f(x)} = f(x)$]

Therefore, solution of the given equation is given by

$$y \cdot x^2 = \int (x) (x^2) dx + C = \int x^3 dx + C$$

or

$$y = \frac{x^2}{4} + C x^{-2}$$

which is the general solution of the given differential equation.

Solution The given equation is a linear differential equation of the type $\frac{dy}{dx} + \text{Py} = \text{Q}$ ,

$$\text{I.F} = e^{\int \cot x \, dx} = e^{\log \sin x} = \sin x$$

$$\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} - 2a \frac{dy}{dx} + (a^2 + b^2) y = 0$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution The given function is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$y = e^{ax} [c_1 \cos bx + c_2 \sin bx] \qquad \dots (1)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Differentiating both sides of equation (1) with respect to $x$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = e^{ax} [-bc_1 \sin bx + bc_2 \cos bx] + [c_1 \cos bx + c_2 \sin bx] e^{ax} \cdot a $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{ax}[(bc_2 + ac_1)\cos bx + (ac_2 - bc_1)\sin bx]$ ... (2)

blocks.label: Paragraph

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = e^{ax}[(bc_2 + ac_1)(-b\sin bx) + (ac_2 - bc_1)(b\cos bx)]$$
$$+ [(bc_2 + ac_1)\cos bx + (ac_2 - bc_1)\sin bx]e^{ax}.a$$
$$= e^{ax}[(a^2c_2 - 2abc_1 - b^2c_2)\sin bx + (a^2c_1 + 2abc_2 - b^2c_1)\cos bx]$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting the values of $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$, $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $y$ in the given differential equation, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
L.H.S. $= e^{ax}[a^2c_2-2abc_1-b^2c_2)\sin bx+(a^2c_1+2abc_2-b^2c_1)\cos bx]$

$-2ae^{ax}[(bc_2+ac_1)\cos bx+(ac_2-bc_1)\sin bx]$

$+(a^2+b^2)e^{ax}[c_1\cos bx+c_2\sin bx]$

$= e^{ax}\left[\begin{array}{l}\left(a^2c_2-2abc_1-b^2c_2-2a^2c_2+2abc_1+a^2c_2+b^2c_2\right)\sin bx\\ +(a^2c_1+2abc_2-b^2c_1-2abc_2-2a^2c_1+a^2c_1+b^2c_1)\cos bx\end{array}\right]$

Example 21 Solve the differential equation

$$ (x \ dy - y \ dx) \ y \ \sin \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) = (y \ dx + x \ dy) \ x \ \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right). $$

Solution The given differential equation can be written as

$$ \left[ x \ y \sin \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) - x^2 \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \right] dy = \left[ xy \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) + y^2 \sin \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \right] dx $$

or

$$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{xy \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) + y^2 \sin \left( \frac{y}{x} \right)}{xy \sin \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) - x^2 \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right)} $$

Dividing numerator and denominator on RHS by $x^2$, we get

$$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{y}{x} \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) + \left( \frac{y^2}{x^2} \right) \sin \left( \frac{y}{x} \right)}{\frac{y}{x} \sin \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) - \cos \left( \frac{y}{x} \right)} \qquad \dots (1) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Clearly, equation (1) is a homogeneous differential equation of the form $\frac{dy}{dx} = g \left( \frac{y}{x} \right).$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: To solve it, we make the substitution

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$y = vx \hspace{12em} \dots (2)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x \frac{dv}{dx}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$v + x \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v \cos v + v^2 \sin v}{v \sin v - \cos v}$$ (using (1) and (2))

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $x \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{2v \cos v}{v \sin v - \cos v}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\left(\frac{v \sin v - \cos v}{v \cos v}\right) dv = \frac{2 dx}{x}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $\int \left( \frac{v \sin v - \cos v}{v \cos v} \right) dv = 2 \int \frac{1}{x} dx$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$\int \tan v \, dv - \int \frac{1}{v} \, dv = 2 \int \frac{1}{x} \, dx$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\log |\sec v| - \log |v| = 2 \log |x| + \log |C_1|$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\log \left| \frac{\sec v}{v x^2} \right| = \log |C_1|$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
or
$$ \frac{\sec v}{v x^2} = \pm C_1 \qquad \dots (3) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\frac{\sec\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)(x^2)} = C \text{ where, } C = \pm C_1$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\sec \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) = C \ xy$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the general solution of the given differential equation.

occurring in the differential equation.
$\diamond$ Degree of a differential equation is defined if it is a polynomial equation in its
derivatives.
$\diamond$ Degree (when defined) of a differential equation is the highest power (positive
integer only) of the highest order derivative in it.
$\diamond$ A function which satisfies the given differential equation is called its solution.
The solution which contains as many arbitrary constants as the order of the
differential equation is called a general solution and the solution free from
arbitrary constants is called particular solution.
$\diamond$ Variable separable method is used to solve such an equation in which variables
can be separated completely i.e. terms containing $y$ should remain with $dy$
and terms containing $x$ should remain with $dx$.
$\diamond$ A differential equation which can be expressed in the form
$\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)$ or $\frac{dx}{dy} = g(x, y)$ where, $f(x, y)$ and $g(x, y)$ are homogenous
functions of degree zero is called a homogeneous differential equation.
$\diamond$ A differential equation of the form $\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$, where P and Q are constants
or functions of $x$ only is called a first order linear differential equation.

Historical Note

One of the principal languages of Science is that of differential equations.
Interestingly, the date of birth of differential equations is taken to be November,
11,1675, when Gottfried Wilthelm Freiherr Leibnitz (1646 - 1716) first put in black

and white the identity $\int y dy = \frac{1}{2} y^2$, thereby introducing both the symbols $\int$ and $dy$.

Leibnitz was actually interested in the problem of finding a curve whose tangents
were prescribed. This led him to discover the ‘method of separation of variables’
1691. A year later he formulated the ‘method of solving the homogeneous

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
*differential equations of the first order*'. He went further in a very short time
to the discovery of the ‘method of solving a linear differential equation of the
first-order’. How surprising is it that all these methods came from a single man
and that too within 25 years of the birth of differential equations!

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the old days, what we now call the ‘solution’ of a differential equation, was
used to be referred to as ‘integral’ of the differential equation, the word being
coined by James Bernoulli (1654 - 1705) in 1690. The word ‘solution was first
used by Joseph Louis Lagrange (1736 - 1813) in 1774, which was almost hundred
years since the birth of differential equations. It was Jules Henri Poincare
(1854 - 1912) who strongly advocated the use of the word ‘solution’ and thus the
word ‘solution’ has found its deserved place in modern terminology. The name of
the ‘method of separation of variables’ is due to John Bernoulli (1667 - 1748),
a younger brother of James Bernoulli.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Application to geometric problems were also considered. It was again John
Bernoulli who first brought into light the intricate nature of differential equations.
In a letter to Leibnitz, dated May 20, 1715, he revealed the solutions of the
differential equation

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
which led to three types of curves, viz., parabolas, hyperbolas and a class of
cubic curves. This shows how varied the solutions of such innocent looking
differential equation can be. From the second half of the twentieth century attention
has been drawn to the investigation of this complicated nature of the solutions of
differential equations, under the heading ‘qualitative analysis of differential
equations’. Now-a-days, this has acquired prime importance being absolutely
necessary in almost all investigations.
